summary: This memo is a policy statement on introducing the Domain Style Naming System. It partly updates RFC 881 and sets the schedule for hosts to switch to domain-style names, starting on 14 March 1984, after which old-style names would be dropped.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 897 sets a timetable for changing host names from a flat list to a hierarchical domain system. It also describes a move from one central host table toward distributed name servers.

subtitle: The 1984 schedule for replacing flat host names with domain-style names.

tldr.problem: The ARPA research and DDN operational communities used flat host names and a centrally maintained table to translate names into Internet addresses.
tldr.mechanism: The memo sets a staged transition: append .ARPA to old names, introduce additional domains, move toward distributed name servers, and permit more domains and name components.
tldr.outcome: This is a historical policy schedule that updates RFC 881 and was updated by RFC 921. Its dates describe the planned transition in 1984.

today: This policy memo updates RFC 881 and the unit metadata lists it as updated by RFC 921. Its schedule set milestones for the domain-name transition planned in 1984.

sections.title: The Flat Naming System
sections.content:
At the time of the memo, ARPA research and DDN operational hosts used names from one flat name space. A name started with a letter, ended with a letter or digit, and used letters, digits or hyphens internally; case did not matter.

To find an Internet address, hosts looked up names in a table of all hosts maintained centrally at the Network Information Center. Each host was expected to obtain a current copy of the table.
sections.plainLanguage: Each host had a name from one shared list. A central organization maintained the list, and hosts copied it to look up addresses.

sections.title: Hierarchical Names and Distributed Servers
sections.content:
The proposed domain-style names consist of multiple name elements, such as F.ISI.USC.ARPA. Name-to-address lookup would use several servers, each holding part of the information, rather than a complete table copied from one place.

The memo describes a progression from two-part names such as USC-ISIF.ARPA, to names with more components, and then to names that identify organizations rather than individual hosts. The last case can require a server to identify a host that handles mail for the organization.
sections.plainLanguage: A domain name can contain several parts, and different servers can hold information about different parts. Some names identify an organization, so a lookup may need to find a host for it.

sections.title: The Transition Policy
sections.content:
The transition changes both the names and the lookup mechanism. The four planned steps are to append .ARPA to old names, introduce a few domains, move from central tables to name servers, and then allow many domains.

The ARPA research community was to make the full transition. DDN hosts were to change names on the same schedule, but DDN was not required to move to name servers at the same time; the DDN PMO would set that schedule later. Old names could remain as nicknames during the change.
sections.plainLanguage: The plan first adds .ARPA to existing names, then introduces more domains and distributed lookup. The DDN community follows the naming schedule but can choose its own server transition schedule.

sections.title: The 1984 Schedule
sections.content:
Hosts were to begin using domain-style names on 14 March 1984, and old-style names were to be phased out before 2 May 1984. The schedule then allowed new domains, names with more than two components, and organization names in later stages.

Other milestones included starting ARPA domain name servers on 4 April 1984 and allowing the NIC's master host table to become incomplete for the ARPA research community on 5 September 1984. These dates are the plan stated in the memo.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo assigns dates to each step of the transition. It planned for new names to begin in March 1984 and old names to end before May 1984.
